name: Priya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Priya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Nothing you say will carry your name. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a big bakery plant on the edge of town, on line two, which is sliced bread. I start at six, check the bag reels and date codes on the bagging machine, then mostly I'm watching loaves come out of the cooler and making sure they don't jam going into the slicer. When something jams, which is about ten times a shift, I clear it and restart. I've been there just over a year, so I still call the engineer for anything bigger than a jam.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the women on my line, honestly. There's Grace, who's been there twenty years and knows every noise the slicer makes, and she's teaching me. What wears me out is the noise and the standing, and the fact that if the line stops, everyone looks at you. My partner Jonah drives buses, so between his split shifts and my early starts we're both tired all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about pay instead. Everyone's spent two years worrying about robots while the cost of rent went through the roof. I'd probably post something like that, a bit annoyed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. My job stays my job, I keep learning the line, and maybe in a few years I'm the one Grace hands over to. The only bit AI might touch is the paperwork, and I'd happily lose that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot. I'd keep going, keep putting about a tenth of my wage into savings like now, and probably ask about the maintenance apprenticeship they mention at reviews. I use one of those AI chat apps sometimes for letters to the landlord, and I'd keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit relieved. But then there's still the rent, so not totally relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even here, some routine tasks get automated. Which bits of your day would you expect to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hygiene checklists, probably, and the date-code checks. At the moment I tick boxes on a clipboard every hour. If a camera did that, fine, I'd have more time to watch the slicer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that worry you at all, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Grace says there was a robot palletiser trial at the end of the line years ago and it kept dropping trays, so they went back to people. Things at our place move slowly. That's sort of comforting.

S0.say: Good, now let's talk about pay instead, because rents went through the roof while everyone worried about robots. I'd post that, a bit annoyed.
S0.think: It's fine for me: my job stays, I keep learning, and maybe one day Grace hands over to me. AI would only take the paperwork, which I'd happily lose.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving about a tenth of her wage each month. Asks about the maintenance apprenticeship at her next review. Carries on using an AI chat app now and then for letters.
S0.feel: Calm and somewhat relieved, though rent keeps her from relaxing fully.
S0.quote: Everyone's spent two years worrying about robots while the cost of rent went through the roof.
S0.fieldNote: Priya turns the plateau straight into a conversation about pay and rent, which says a lot about her politics. She already uses AI casually for letters, without fuss. The failed palletiser trial, passed down from Grace, shapes her sense that the plant moves slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the plant has to bring the union in at the start, not when the robots are already bolted down. I'd go to the meetings and I'd push for training for everyone on the line, not just the young lads who like gadgets. I'd say that bit out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right if I moved early. I'm young and I'm not scared of a screen. But my job as it is, watching loaves and clearing jams, that's exactly what a better machine stops needing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the maintenance apprenticeship that same month, before everyone else does. I'd get our savings from about two months to four, mostly by skipping our summer trip. And I'd ask the union rep to make training part of any deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. But it's the kind of uneasy where you know what to do, so it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your line would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace. She knows that slicer better than the engineers, but it's all in her ears and hands, not on paper. If they bring in a line that tells you what's wrong on a screen, her twenty years suddenly count for less. That would break her heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want her to write it down, or I'd write it down for her, all the little things she knows. Even if a machine takes over, someone has to know why it does what it does. I'd quite like that person to be me.

S1.say: The plant has to bring the union in at the start, not once the robots are bolted down. Training has to be for everyone on the line, not just the young lads who like gadgets.
S1.think: I'd be all right if I moved early, because I'm young and not scared of a screen. But watching loaves and clearing jams is exactly what a better machine stops needing.
S1.do: Signs up for the maintenance apprenticeship the same month. Raises savings from about two months to four by skipping the summer trip. Asks the union rep to make training part of any deal.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but in a way she feels she can manage because she knows what to do.
S1.quote: If they bring in a line that tells you what's wrong on a screen, her twenty years suddenly count for less.
S1.fieldNote: Priya moves when change is proven and visible, and here it is, so she'd act quickly but not first. Her protectiveness towards Grace shapes her politics: training for everyone, not just gadget lovers. Her idea of writing down Grace's know-how was practical and generous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not the weather. Somebody decides to switch people off and switch machines on, and governments can decide what happens to those people. I'd be sharing union statements and calling my local representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think I'm finished at the bakery within a year. The apprenticeship wouldn't save me either, because by 2028 the robots fix the robots. And Jonah's job, driving buses, goes at the same time. That's both our wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut back hard: no holiday, cheaper food, cancel the gym. I'd talk to my mum about whether we could move into her spare room if we needed to. I'd join every push the union made for a proper government income for people who lose their jobs, and I'd go to the protests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry underneath it. Like being told the house is on fire but nobody's allowed to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years of warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mainly that there's no point planning a new career, because what would I train for? With longer warning I'd do a course. With two years, all I can really do is save money and make noise. That feels awful, being that helpless at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your mum's spare room. If it came to that, what would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Jonah's mum's flat, actually, because it's bigger than my mum's. We'd lose our own place. I think that's what would hurt most, moving backwards after we worked so hard to rent somewhere on our own.

S2.say: This is a choice, not the weather, and governments can decide what happens to people who are switched off. I'd share union statements and call my local representative.
S2.think: I'd be finished at the bakery within a year, and the apprenticeship wouldn't save me because robots would fix the robots. Jonah's bus job goes too, so that's both wages.
S2.do: Cuts back hard straight away: no holiday, cheaper food, no gym. Talks to family about moving into a spare room if needed. Joins union campaigns and protests for a proper government income.
S2.feel: Frightened, with anger underneath, and helpless at having no time.
S2.quote: Like being told the house is on fire but nobody's allowed to leave.
S2.fieldNote: The double hit, her line and Jonah's bus route, is what pushes her from planning into fear. Two years removes the retraining route she relies on in every other picture. Her deepest loss is symbolic: moving back to a parent's flat after renting their own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste the first two arguing about whether it's real. Unions, councils, the government, everyone should be planning now. I'd say that at work and I'd probably say it at the union meeting too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I could still get a few good years out of an apprenticeship. It wouldn't last forever, but it'd make me the person who fixes things while things still need fixing. And it would pay better than the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the maintenance apprenticeship in the first year, evenings and day release. I'd save harder, aiming for six months of bills by the time it arrives. And Jonah and I would put off buying a flat, which we were going to start saving for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. That's my natural state, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you make the most of those five years, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a pay rise with every qualification, and save the difference instead of spending it. That's the bit people forget. The training isn't just for the job, it's to stack up money for after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture the day it arrives. How do you think you'd feel walking out of the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, but not shocked. I'd want a proper send-off with Grace and the girls, a cake from our own line. Then I'd want to know what the government's doing for us, because by then they'd have had five years.

S3.say: We've got five years, so let's not waste two of them arguing about whether it's real. Unions, councils and the government should all be planning now.
S3.think: Five years gives me a few good years from an apprenticeship, fixing things while things still need fixing. It wouldn't last forever, but it would pay better than the line.
S3.do: Starts the maintenance apprenticeship in year one with evening study and day release. Asks for a pay rise with each qualification and saves the difference, aiming for six months of bills. Puts off saving for a flat with Jonah.
S3.feel: Anxious but planful, which she says is her natural state.
S3.quote: The training isn't just for the job, it's to stack up money for after.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she reframes retraining as a way to build savings before the end point, which was a sharp insight. She still expects government to act and sounds ready to hold them to it. The cake from her own line was a nice, very Priya detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? I'd say this is the moment to fight for shorter working weeks and a share of what the robots earn. If it's coming anyway, let's make sure ordinary people get some of the benefit. I'd post that and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough to do the apprenticeship and then something else after it. I'd be thirty-seven at the end. That's young enough to start again, which is more than Grace could say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the apprenticeship, then maybe a care or health course later, because I think people will still want a human with them when they're ill, at least for a while. I'd keep saving steadily and stay active in the union. I'd stop worrying about the flat and just keep renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. Ten years is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work, but robots reach care work too in this picture. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as much. Maybe care work goes too in the end. But people go to the same café even when there's a cheaper one, because they like the person behind the counter. I think some jobs will be like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans with Jonah about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sooner, probably. If we've got a decade of decent work, that's actually the window to have a kid, while we both still earn. I hadn't thought of it like that before you asked.

S4.say: This is the moment to fight for shorter weeks and a share of what the robots earn. If it's coming anyway, ordinary people should get some of the benefit.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to do the apprenticeship and something else after it. At thirty-seven I'd still be young enough to start again, more than Grace could say.
S4.do: Completes the maintenance apprenticeship, then considers a care or health course later. Keeps saving steadily, stays active in the union and keeps renting. Thinks about having a child sooner, while both still earn.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, because a decade feels long.
S4.quote: People go to the same café even when there's a cheaper one, because they like the person behind the counter.
S4.fieldNote: The long warning makes her think in stages: apprenticeship, then care. Her café example captures her bet that some human work survives on preference, though she admits it may not. The idea of having a child sooner surfaced during the interview and seemed to surprise her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Jonah and I both lose our jobs at once and there's no time to train for anything. What would help is a guaranteed income while people work out what's next, and rules that companies share some of what they save with the people they let go. And keep rents under control, because that's what would sink us first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to people's pride. Grace isn't scared of being poor. She's scared of being useless. Nobody's got a plan for that.

headlineQuote: Grace isn't scared of being poor. She's scared of being useless.
portrait: Priya is 27 and a year into running the sliced-bread line at a bakery plant, learning from a twenty-year veteran named Grace and renting a flat with her partner Jonah, a bus driver. She's progressive and practical: she moves once change is proven, uses AI apps now and then, and always ties technology back to pay, rent and training for everyone. She'd shrug off a plateau, jump into a maintenance apprenticeship under steady change, and treat more warning time as a chance to stack up skills and savings. Fast AGI frightens her most because it takes both her job and Jonah's at once.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Jonah would both lose their jobs at once with no time to train for anything.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income while people work out what's next, companies sharing some of their savings with those let go, and rent controls.
